guide.title: How HTTP Requests Work on the Web
guide.text:
## How HTTP Requests Work on the Web

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the basic way browsers and servers exchange data. A client, e.g. a browser or mobile app, sends an **HTTP request** to a server, and the server returns an **HTTP response**. This usually happens over **HTTPS** (HTTP + TLS), which encrypts the traffic.

### Request Basics

A request has a few main parts:

- **Method**: what action to perform  
  - `GET` = fetch data  
  - `POST` = send new data  
  - `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` = update or remove data
- **URL**: the resource location, e.g. `https://api.example.com/v1/users`
- **Headers**: metadata like `Content-Type: application/json`, `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- **Body**: optional data sent with `POST`, `PUT`, etc.

A typical flow is:

`browser -> DNS lookup -> connect to server -> send request -> receive response`

### Response Basics

The server replies with:

- **Status code**
  - `200 OK` = success
  - `201 Created` = new resource made
  - `400 Bad Request` = client error
  - `401 Unauthorized` = missing/invalid auth
  - `404 Not Found` = resource does not exist
  - `500 Internal Server Error` = server problem
- **Headers**: e.g. `Content-Type: application/json`
- **Body**: the data, often JSON or HTML

### Worked Example

Request:

```http
GET /v1/users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
```

Response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":42,"name":"Ava"}
```

This means the client asked for user `42`, and the server returned JSON successfully.

### Quick Notes

- HTTP is stateless: each request is independent.
- Performance matters: a site with 99.9% uptime can still feel slow if latency is high.
- Large responses may be split into chunks; 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MiB.

script.title: HTTP Requests Basics: How Browsers Talk to Servers
script.description: Learn the core parts of an HTTP request and response, how HTTPS adds encryption, and how status codes and headers shape what you get back.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Welcome back. Today we are talking about how HTTP requests work on the web, in plain terms. When you open a browser page or use a mobile app, a client sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server replies with an HTTP response. Usually that happens over HTTPS, which is HTTP plus TLS, so the traffic is encrypted.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Right, and it helps to picture the whole conversation as one request at a time. A request has a few main parts. First is the method, which is the action you want. GET fetches data. POST sends new data. PUT, PATCH, and DELETE update or remove data.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Next is the URL, which is the resource location. For example, https://api.example.com/v1/users. Then we have headers, which are metadata. Common ones include Content-Type set to application/json, and Authorization set to Bearer plus a token. Finally there is the body, which is optional data you send with POST, PUT, or similar methods.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: And there is a typical flow. The browser does a DNS lookup, then connects to the server, then sends the request, then receives the response. Quick question for you, hostA: why do you think headers matter so much compared to just the URL?

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Because headers carry extra instructions and context. Like Content-Type tells the server what format you are sending or expecting, and Authorization tells the server how you are allowed to access something. Without those, the server might not interpret the request correctly or might reject it.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Exactly. Now let’s switch to the response side. The server replies with a status code, headers, and a body. The status code is the big signal about what happened. For example, 200 OK means success. 201 Created means a new resource was made. 400 Bad Request is a client error. 401 Unauthorized means missing or invalid auth. 404 Not Found means the resource does not exist. 500 Internal Server Error means the server had a problem.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Headers in the response can include Content-Type, like application/json, and the body is the data, often JSON or HTML. Key idea: HTTP is stateless, so each request is independent. That means the server does not automatically remember your previous request state unless you build that into the app.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: Let’s make it concrete with the worked example. The request is a GET for a specific user. It looks like this in concept: GET for the path v one slash users slash forty two, with Host set to api dot example dot com, and Accept set to application slash json.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: Then the response shows HTTP slash one dot one, then 200 OK, then Content-Type as application slash json, and a JSON body like id equals forty two and name equals Ava. So the client asked for user forty two, and the server returned JSON successfully.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: One more practical note: performance matters. Even if a site has 99.9 percent uptime, it can still feel slow if latency is high. Also, large responses may be split into chunks. The source mentions that one MiB is one million forty eight thousand five hundred seventy six bytes, which is 1,048,576 bytes.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostA
transcriptTurns.text: So if I summarize the request parts: method tells the action, URL points to the resource, headers provide metadata like content type and authorization, and the body carries optional data. And on the response side: status code tells success or specific errors, headers describe the response, and the body contains the data.

transcriptTurns.speaker: hostB
transcriptTurns.text: And the main takeaway is that every interaction is a request and response pair. HTTPS encrypts the traffic, status codes guide your next step, and statelessness means each request stands on its own. That is the foundation for understanding APIs and web communication.
